article.title: When Better Forecasts Do Not Produce Better Decisions
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Organizations often assume that a more accurate forecast will automatically produce a better business outcome. If a demand model predicts sales more precisely, inventory should improve. If a churn model ranks customers more accurately, retention should rise. If a risk model estimates default more precisely, lending decisions should become better. The logic is appealing, but it skips a crucial step: a forecast creates value only when it changes a decision in a useful way.

Consider inventory planning. A retailer improves weekly demand forecast error from 18 percent to 12 percent. That sounds substantial. Yet suppliers require orders eight weeks in advance, minimum order quantities are large, and warehouse capacity is fixed. If the improved forecast arrives only one week before sales occur, planners may have no practical action available. Predictive accuracy improved, but decision value barely changed.

This distinction matters because model evaluation and decision evaluation answer different questions. Forecast metrics ask whether predictions resemble eventual outcomes. Decision metrics ask whether using those predictions changes actions and improves economic results. A model can win on mean absolute error, AUC, or another technical measure while producing little incremental value in the actual workflow.

One reason is that decisions are often threshold-based. A retention team may contact only the top 5 percent of customers because call-center capacity is limited. Improving predictions for customers ranked far below that cutoff has almost no operational value. What matters is whether the new model changes the composition of the actionable group and whether those changes identify customers who can actually be influenced.

Actionability creates another constraint. A model may correctly predict that a customer will leave because the customer is moving abroad. The prediction is accurate, but a retention offer may not change the outcome. By contrast, a slightly less certain customer who is unhappy with service quality may be highly persuadable. Prediction of behavior and prediction of treatment response are different problems. Organizations can waste resources when they target the people most likely to experience an outcome rather than the people whose outcome can be changed.

Decision costs also matter. Suppose a fraud model catches more suspicious transactions but increases false positives. If every flagged transaction requires manual investigation, the new model may overwhelm the review team. The economic question is not whether recall increased in isolation, but whether the value of additional fraud prevented exceeds investigation costs, customer friction, and losses from incorrectly blocked transactions.

Timing can dominate accuracy as well. A moderately accurate forecast delivered early enough to influence procurement may be more valuable than a highly accurate forecast delivered after purchasing decisions are locked. This suggests that data latency, decision lead time, and operational response time belong in the evaluation framework alongside predictive metrics.

The same principle applies to uncertainty. A point forecast of 1,000 units may appear precise, but a planner may need to know whether plausible demand ranges from 950 to 1,050 or from 500 to 1,500. Two forecasts with similar average error can imply very different safety-stock decisions. Communicating uncertainty can therefore improve decisions even when headline accuracy does not change.

A useful evaluation starts by mapping the decision process backward. What decision will be made? When must it be made? Which actions are available? What constraints limit those actions? What are the costs of false positives, false negatives, delay, and intervention? Only then should teams decide which model metric is most relevant. This prevents the common mistake of optimizing a convenient technical score that is weakly connected to business value.

Experiments can provide stronger evidence than offline accuracy alone. If a new ranking model changes which customers receive an offer, a controlled test can measure incremental retention or profit. If a demand forecast changes replenishment, teams can compare stockouts, waste, and working capital. The model becomes one component of a decision system rather than an isolated prediction engine.

This perspective also changes how model improvements should be prioritized. Engineers may find a feature that improves AUC by a small amount, but if it does not alter decisions near the operational threshold, its business value may be negligible. Another change that improves calibration around the threshold or delivers predictions two days earlier could be more valuable despite a smaller headline accuracy gain.

Better forecasts are useful, but accuracy is an intermediate objective. The final objective is better action under constraints. Organizations should therefore evaluate the entire chain from data to prediction, from prediction to decision, and from decision to outcome. When that chain is explicit, teams can identify whether the next dollar should be spent on a better model, faster data, more operational capacity, a different intervention, or a better decision rule. The best forecasting system is not necessarily the one that predicts the future most precisely. It is the one that helps the organization make better choices before the future arrives.
paragraphs.zh: 更準確的 forecast 不一定產生更好的 decision，因為預測只有在能改變可執行行動時才創造價值。零售需求模型即使誤差大幅下降，若預測出現時採購早已鎖定，decision value 仍有限。技術指標與決策指標回答不同問題；有限的 call-center capacity、action threshold、供應鏈 lead time 都會限制模型價值。更重要的是，預測誰會流失不等於預測誰能被挽留，behavior prediction 與 treatment response 不同。False positive、人工審查成本、customer friction、timing 與 uncertainty 也必須納入。應從決策反推：何時決定、有哪些 action、有哪些 constraint、錯誤成本是多少，再選模型 metric。最好用實驗衡量 incremental outcome。Accuracy 是中間目標，最終目標是在限制下做出更好的行動。
paragraphs.ja: より正確なforecastが必ずbetter decisionにつながるわけではありません。予測は実際のactionを有益に変えられる場合に価値を生みます。forecastが改善してもprocurementが既にlockされていれば価値は小さいです。technical metricとdecision metricは別で、capacity、threshold、lead timeなどのconstraintが重要です。またchurnを予測することと、誰がinterventionで変化するかを予測することは異なります。false positive、review cost、customer friction、timing、uncertaintyも評価対象です。まずdecision、時点、action、constraint、error costを定義し、その後に適切なmodel metricを選びます。accuracyは中間目標で、最終目標は制約下でより良い行動を選ぶことです。

quiz.question: Why may a more accurate forecast have little value?
quiz.answer: Because it may arrive too late or fail to change an available action.

quiz.question: Why is churn risk different from treatment response?
quiz.answer: High-risk customers are not necessarily the customers whose behavior can be changed.
